passages.where: Daniel's fellow officials look for a charge against him and can find no corruption or negligence, because he is trustworthy. The site's note on the chapter says it was jealousy at his rise that set them plotting. Their only hope, they decide, is something to do with his faith, and the integrity of his work leaves them nothing else.

Joseph, managing his master's house, refuses the advances of his master's wife day after day, and will not even be near her. The site's plain note says he said no again and again to someone who had power over him, and on the verses that follow it says that anyone pressured by a boss or anyone with power over them is not to blame, and that saying no is right even if they punish you for it. Joseph's refusal cost him his post.

The herdsmen of Abram and Lot quarrel because the land cannot hold both households, and Abram asks that there be no contention between them and offers Lot first choice. The site's note says the problem was not hostility but abundance, and that Abram appealed to kinship rather than his rank as the elder. The one with the right to choose first gave it away to keep the peace.

Paul and Barnabas disagree so sharply over taking Mark that they part company and go to different places. The site's plain note says Luke does not hide that two faithful men quarrelled, and that God kept working through both of them. Not every conflict between good colleagues ends in agreement, and a parting is not always a failure.

Paul pleads with two women who had laboured beside him for the gospel to agree with each other in the Lord, and asks a true yokefellow to help them. The site's plain note says Paul names the quarrel but takes no side, and asks whether you could be the one who helps two people at odds. Fellow workers falling out is as old as the church's own work.

The Teacher has seen an error that proceeds from the ruler: folly set in high places while the able sit low. The site's note on the chapter puts it plainly, that fools are promoted while the capable are passed over. Scripture does not pretend that promotion always follows merit.

When the women's song credits David with tens of thousands and Saul with thousands, Saul is furious and keeps a jealous eye on David from that day. The site's note on the chapter says the song turned Saul's admiration into jealousy, and that he twice tried to spear David. David served a jealous superior for a time, and when the spear came he got out of its way, as verse 11 says.

Jesus says that if a brother sins against you, go to him privately, and if he listens you have won him over. The site's plain note says he sends you to the person, not to everyone else about the person, and that these steps are for wrongs between people on roughly equal ground; they do not fit a case where one person has power over another or where someone is afraid. Abuse and crimes go to the proper authorities.

Soldiers ask John the Baptist what they should do, and he tells them not to take money by force or false accusation and to be content with their wages. The site's note says John does not tell them to leave their service but to stop abusing its power, each group hearing the temptation of its own trade. False accusation is named among the sins of a working life.

Paul tells masters to give up their use of threats, because master and servant share one Master in heaven who shows no favoritism. The site's plain note says a worker is not property and a boss is not an owner, that treating workers without threats can be applied to work with care, and that no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work. It asks anyone with power over others whether they use threats, open or quiet.

misread.taken: Servants, submit to your masters, even to those who are unreasonable is used to tell a worker who is being bullied, harassed or threatened that a Christian should stay quiet and put up with it.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Peter writes to slaves with no way out, in an empire that crushed slave revolts, and that within that world he calls their unjust treatment unjust and sets them beside Christ. It says the passage is never a reason to tell someone who is being hurt by another person that they must stay and bear it, and that nothing in it asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. The note on Ephesians 6 adds that a worker is not property and a boss is not an owner.

whole: If someone at work is threatening you, pressuring you for sex, or hurting you, that is not an ordinary conflict, and you do not have to manage it alone: tell someone you trust and get help, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Most conflict at work is less dramatic and still wears people down. A colleague takes credit for your work. A manager plays favourites, or loses their temper in meetings, or never says anything directly. Two departments are at war and everyone is expected to take a side. The promotion goes to someone else. Because work pays the bills, it can feel impossible to say anything, and so the conflict is carried home and replayed at night.

Scripture recognizes all of it. Daniel's colleagues plotted against him out of jealousy. Saul grew jealous of David the day a song praised him more. The Teacher saw fools promoted while capable people sat low. Paul and Barnabas, two good men, disagreed so sharply that they parted, and two women who had worked beside Paul fell out badly enough for him to name them in a letter. Beneath much conflict at work the Bible sees the same things it sees everywhere: rivalry, fear of losing face, and the abuse of power by those who have it over others. It also sees how easily the one who is wronged picks up the same weapons, the gossip, the faction, the quiet sabotage.

So the Bible's wisdom is practical and does not ask for silence about wrong. Where it is safe and the two of you stand on roughly equal ground, go to the person and not to everyone else about them, as Jesus says. Do your work so faithfully that, as with Daniel, an accusation has nothing to land on. Give up the right to win every point, as Abram gave Lot first choice to end the quarrel. Ask someone to help, as Paul asked his true yokefellow to help Euodia and Syntyche. Where the conflict is a person with power using it badly, the steps of Matthew 18 do not fit, and the notes say so; use the proper channels at work and seek advice. If you are the one with power, hear Paul's word to masters: give up threats, for you have a Master too.

The hope Scripture gives is that the God who sees behind every closed door is the judge of every workplace. Joseph lost his post for doing right, and the LORD was with him in the prison. Paul and Barnabas parted, and God worked through both. Your reputation, your promotion and your vindication do not finally rest with a manager or a review. You can do honest work, refuse the easy weapons, speak up where wrong is done, and leave the rest to the one who shows no favoritism.
sit: Is there someone at work you have talked about more than you have talked to, and is it safe to go to them?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says the songs of ascents begin in a place of lies and conflict, among people who want war when you want peace, and that this psalm lets you say so to God. Pray it before a hard day at work.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help.
You are not to blame for their pressure.
But no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
